content:
European Council President António Costa presented a revised plan for the European Union's next seven-year budget on Saturday, cutting spending further and proposing a new tax on large digital companies to help finance it, according to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/eu-leaders-chair-proposes-new-cuts-eu-2028-2034-budget-draft-suggests-digital-2026-11-21/).

The draft would reduce the 2028–2034 budget by €40 billion to €1.582 trillion compared with a compromise proposal put forward by the Irish EU presidency in October, and by €180.6 billion compared with the European Commission's original plan. Costa, who chairs summits of the EU's 27 leaders, told a press conference in Brussels that he believed the proposal "can bring us closer to a final agreement", the South China Morning Post reported.

The cuts fall mainly on the European Competitiveness Fund — the pot designed to help European industry compete with China and the United States — as well as on defence and external spending. Money for agriculture and cohesion, the funds that support farmers and poorer regions, is relatively protected compared with the Irish compromise, Reuters reported.

That did not stop criticism from both ends of the debate. France said the new numbers did not sufficiently protect farmers, while the European Parliament's chief budget negotiator, Siegfried Muresan, called the draft a step backwards. "This proposal is unacceptable to Parliament and cannot form the basis for our consent. The EU budget is an investment budget. Cuts, more cuts and a side of cuts are not an investment strategy," he said, according to Reuters.

The most politically charged element of Costa's package is the proposed digital tax. Under the draft, companies with at least €50 million a year in turnover from digital activities inside the EU and more than €750 million in global turnover would pay an annual contribution of 3% of their net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data. The levy would also be accompanied by a charge on electronic waste and higher tobacco taxes, according to TRT World.

In practice, the tax would fall mostly on US-based digital giants such as Google, Microsoft, Meta, Apple and Amazon. That is precisely why many EU governments have long been wary of it. US President Donald Trump has spoken against digital services taxes, and Washington has in the past threatened tariffs in retaliation against countries that imposed them — France faced that threat in 2019 when it introduced its own levy. Costa's proposal therefore revives a fight Brussels has repeatedly chosen to avoid, and it does so at a moment when the EU is also trying to keep Washington onside over [Ukraine](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/zh/articles/eu-45-billion-euro-loan-ukraine-2027-november-2026) and [trade](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-us-trade-deal-signing-delayed-november-2026).

The idea itself is not new. Costa's proposal builds on a 2018 plan from the European Commission that was never taken up by EU governments, Reuters noted. What has changed since then is the pressure on the budget. The seven-year framework under discussion must now absorb higher energy costs, a sharp rise in defence spending and the cost of servicing the more than €600 billion the EU jointly borrowed for its post-pandemic recovery fund. Costa also proposed slowing the repayment of the capital of that borrowing, with interest and capital repayments running from 2028 to 2058 as planned but the capital element repaid more slowly in the first seven years, to leave more money for other priorities.

The logic of the tax is fiscal as much as political. The EU budget is financed from national contributions and from so-called "own resources" — levies collected by member states but dedicated to the EU budget, such as customs duties, a share of value-added tax and a tax on non-recycled plastic waste. The more own resources the budget has, the less governments must contribute directly from national coffers. A digital levy would therefore ease the burden on national budgets at a time when almost every capital is under strain — but only if all 27 member states agree. Budget decisions and new own resources must be adopted unanimously, and the negotiation is, in Reuters' words, "often an acrimonious battle".

The divisions are familiar. Germany has led calls for substantial cuts to the Commission's original plan, which TRT World reported at close to €2 trillion, while net beneficiaries of EU spending resist reductions to cohesion and farm funds. Costa's draft tries to square that circle by cutting the total while protecting agriculture and cohesion — yet France still objected, and the Parliament, whose consent is required, has already signalled it will not accept the numbers as they stand.

EU leaders will discuss Costa's proposals at a special summit on November 26–27, with the aim of narrowing the gap between net contributors and net beneficiaries and reaching an agreement in December. The timetable is tight for a reason: although the budget only has to be ready for 2028, leaders want a deal by the end of 2026 because elections are due next year in France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland and Slovakia, and the budget is likely to feature in those campaigns.

The digital tax is the clearest test of whether the bloc can still agree on new sources of revenue of its own. If it survives the summit, it would be the EU's first bloc-wide levy aimed squarely at the business model of the American tech giants — and the first time Brussels has been willing to risk a trade row with Washington to pay for its own budget. If it fails, as the 2018 proposal did, the cuts will have to come from somewhere else, and the argument over who pays for Europe's ambitions will simply move to the next summit. For now, Costa has put both the knife and the tax on the table, and given leaders a week to decide which they dislike less.
summary: European Council President António Costa unveiled a revised seven-year EU budget on Saturday, cutting the total to €1.582 trillion and proposing a 3% levy on the digital revenues of large tech firms to help pay for it — a move that would fall mostly on US giants and risks a confrontation with Washington.
title: EU's Costa proposes 3% tax on Big Tech to fund slimmer €1.58 trillion budget
